title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest covers your five tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Findings are pulled from recent PubMed/PMC, JAMA, NIH/ClinicalTrials.gov, Frontiers, Nature, Springer, and AASM sources, with citations linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
This week's signal: **be selective**. A fresh 2026 comparative review stacked the three most-hyped "longevity supplements" against each other and found they are *not* interchangeable.

- **Urolithin A leads the pack.** The review (covering RCTs through April 2026) concluded urolithin A has the **most coherent human evidence** — mechanism, biomarkers, and early functional gains all align for mitochondrial health, muscle endurance, and immune aging. **NAD+ precursors (NR/NMN)** reliably raise NAD+ biomarkers but functional benefits remain *inconsistent*, and **spermidine** is biologically plausible but still clinically unvalidated.
- **Taurine — biomarkers, not proof.** The 6-month **TauAge RCT** (4 g/day, adults 55–75) finished in late 2025; a 2025 systematic review of 34 RCTs found taurine may improve **cardiometabolic markers** (best at 1.5–3 g/day), but there is still **no evidence it slows biological aging or extends lifespan** in humans.
- **Senolytics stay investigational.** A 2026 pharmacology review notes fewer than ten human senolytic studies exist. In postmenopausal women, dasatinib + quercetin improved **bone density only in those with the highest senescent-cell burden** — a hint that senolytics may need to be *personalized* to an aging biomarker rather than taken broadly.
- **Devices — red/near-infrared light.** A randomized, sham-controlled trial of a home **630 nm LED + 850 nm near-infrared mask** found **86% of users improved crow's feet vs. 17%** with the sham over 12–16 weeks. A 2026 ex-vivo + clinical study of a similar mask + cream showed measurable rises in **collagen I and elastin** and ~24% less crow's-feet wrinkle depth at day 56. Use eye protection and follow device instructions.

Practical framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-supplement "reverse aging" claims with skepticism.

sources.title: Urolithin A, Spermidine, and NAD+ Precursors in Human Healthy Aging: A Comparative Narrative Review of Recent Clinical Evidence

Home-used LED and IRED mask for crow's feet: a multi-center, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study
Anti-Aging Efficacy of a Home-use Red and Infrared LED Mask and a Cream: Ex Vivo and Clinical Evaluations in Women With Mature Skin

sections.body:
New 2026 meta-analyses reinforce HIIT as a **time-efficient cardio and fat-loss tool** for women — with a consistent caveat that it does less for strength and lean mass.

- **Middle-aged & older women.** A 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis of **19 RCTs** found HIIT produced a **large, high-certainty improvement in VO2max** (SMD 1.20) but **no significant gains in muscle strength** and only borderline walking-ability improvement. Translation: HIIT is excellent for the heart and lungs, but **not sufficient on its own** for functional strength.
- **Overweight/obesity.** A 2026 meta-analysis of **15 RCTs** in women with overweight/obesity showed HIIT significantly cut **body weight, BMI, body-fat %, and fat mass**, raised VO2max (g 1.09), and nudged **HDL up / LDL down**; effects on total cholesterol and triglycerides were not significant.
- **How it ranks vs. other exercise.** A 2026 network meta-analysis (43 RCTs, 2,315 women) found HIIT ranked **best for fat-mass reduction**, while vigorous aerobic exercise led for BMI and body-fat %. **No modality meaningfully improved lean mass except resistance training** — another vote for pairing HIIT with strength work.
- **Postmenopausal metabolic angle.** In a network meta-analysis of 51 RCTs, HIIT ranked **highest for triglyceride lowering** (tentative sweet spot ~1,000–1,300 MET-min/week), though based on few studies.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and adiposity wins; **add 2–3 resistance sessions/week**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sources.title: Effects of HIIT on Cardiopulmonary Fitness and Physical Function in Middle-aged and Elderly Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). The newest 2026 trials sharpen two questions: *is Pilates a substitute?* and *does intensity matter?*

- **PFMT beats Pilates.** A 3-arm RCT (105 women, published Oct 2026) compared Pilates, Pilates + voluntary pelvic-floor contraction, and PFMT over 6 weeks. **PFMT was clearly superior** — incontinence impact (ICIQ-SF) fell **−4.4 points vs. only −0.7** for both Pilates groups, with much larger gains in muscle strength and squeeze pressure. Pilates is a nice adjunct, **not a replacement** for targeted training.
- **Postmenopausal women.** A smaller 2026 RCT found PFMT improved **muscle strength and nighttime voiding** more than mat Pilates with contraction cueing, but the two were **similar for incontinence severity and leakage** — reinforcing that technique-specific training builds the muscle, even when symptom scores converge.
- **Intensity counts (postpartum).** In 99 women with postpartum SUI, a **high-intensity combined protocol** (focused *plus* generalized PFMT) produced the greatest strength gains and the **lowest 6-month recurrence** — efficacy tracked with training intensity.
- **Add relaxation for comfort.** A four-arm RCT found pairing PFMT with **progressive muscle relaxation** improved patient-reported comfort beyond exercises alone.

Key point: **correct activation + consistency + adequate intensity** drive results. Confirm your technique with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones.

sources.title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training Outperforms Pilates in Women with Stress Urinary Incontinence: A Randomized Controlled Trial

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard HER2-targeted therapy** — not a replacement. Two honest themes this week: one promising, one cautionary.

- **Correct vitamin D deficiency (promising).** A 2026 retrospective *interventional* study (196 early-stage HER2+ patients on trastuzumab) found that **failing to correct vitamin D deficiency carried a 1.7× higher recurrence risk**, with the best disease-free-survival trends in those reaching D25 >50 ng/mL (a dose-response signal). The effect didn't reach statistical significance in this underpowered cohort, but a sister cohort did, and two 2025 RCTs reported a **doubling of pathologic complete response** with repletion — strongest in HER2+ and triple-negative disease. Note the genetic link: **germline TP53 mutations** make HER2+ the most likely subtype (~67%), so genetics matter in this group.
- **Curcumin (cautionary).** A 2026 meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (945 patients) found curcumin **did not improve tumor response, quality of life, fatigue, or pain** — its one moderate-certainty benefit was **less severe radiation dermatitis** (RR 0.51). An earlier randomized trial adding curcumin to docetaxel in metastatic disease was **stopped for futility**. Bioavailability and herb–drug interactions remain real limits.
- **Supplements broadly.** A 2026 Frontiers in Oncology translational review maps curcumin, resveratrol, quercetin, luteolin, and withaferin A across subtypes, but concludes robust clinical efficacy evidence is still **limited** and flags **interaction risk with targeted therapy**.

Important framing: much of this is **early or observational**. Use integrative options as *clinician-coordinated add-ons* — never as substitutes for HER2-targeted treatment — and check every supplement against your current regimen.

sources.title: Successful Vitamin D Replacement After Deficiency and Disease-Free Survival in Curative-Intent HER2+ Breast Cancer: A Retrospective Interventional Study
Effects of Curcumin on Treatment-Related Toxicities and Patient-Reported Outcomes in Breast Cancer: Systematic Review & Meta-analysis of RCTs
Curcumin's Effect in Advanced/Metastatic Breast Cancer Treated with Docetaxel: A Randomized Trial (stopped for futility)
Natural Supplements in Breast Cancer Therapy: Translational Evidence, Clinical Safety, and Emerging Challenges

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or fragmented sleep, 2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I stays first-line.** The AASM's 2026 clinical practice guideline on *combination* therapy made two conditional recommendations: CBT-I **plus** medication is suggested over **medication alone**, but combination is **not** suggested over **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I delivers durable improvement without drug risks. Start with the behavioral foundation.
- **Melatonin is not a general sleeping pill.** A 2026 Frontiers review stresses melatonin should **not be used as a broad hypnotic** for insomnia; it's most useful for **circadian problems** (phase delay, jet lag, shift work) rather than chronic sleep-maintenance insomnia. A new RCT (**SOAM**, recruiting, adults ≥60) is testing whether 3 mg melatonin *added to CBT-I* improves outcomes — results are years out.
- **Magnesium — modest and uncertain.** A 2026 systematic review of RCTs concluded current evidence **does not support routine magnesium** for insomnia; benefits were inconsistent and of low/very-low certainty. Reasonable to consider only if dietary intake is low.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends — it's the strongest circadian anchor.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window; get morning daylight.
4. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or a validated digital program).
